title: Which eviction policy would you choose for this cache, and why?
summary: Tests whether you can match an eviction policy to an actual access pattern instead of defaulting to "LRU, obviously."

slides.markdown:
"LRU, obviously" is the reflex answer, and it's often wrong. **LRU** (least recently used) evicts whatever hasn't been touched in the longest time — a great fit when recency predicts future access, and a poor fit when it doesn't. The interviewer wants you to check that assumption against the actual access pattern before naming a policy.

The strong answer names the access pattern first, then picks the policy that matches it.

Ask: **is access recency-driven or frequency-driven — do the same few keys dominate over time, or does what's hot shift constantly?** If yesterday's popular keys are still today's popular keys, frequency is the better signal. If what's hot changes rapidly and recent access is the best predictor of near-future access, recency wins.

This one question separates the cases where LRU is genuinely right from the cases where it quietly underperforms.

Match the policy to the pattern: **LRU** for recency-driven access (a general-purpose cache where "recently touched" reliably predicts "will be touched again"). **LFU** (least frequently used) for a stable hot set, where the same items stay popular over a long window and raw recency is a worse predictor than accumulated popularity. **TTL-based eviction** for time-bound relevance, where an item's usefulness genuinely expires regardless of how often it's accessed.

Name the pattern, then the policy — never the reverse.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a trending-content cache where LFU beats LRU
slides.markdown:
| | LRU | LFU |
|---|---|---|
| Signal used | Most recent access time | Total access count |
| Behavior on a viral one-off read | Treats it as "just accessed," keeps it warm | Correctly treats it as low-frequency, evicts it first |
| Fit for a trending-content cache | Poor — a single burst can look as "hot" as sustained popularity | Good — sustained popularity accumulates a real count |

**How to decide:** recency is a poor proxy for what's actually popular whenever a single burst of access can look identical to sustained demand — that's exactly the trending-content case, where LFU's accumulated count tells a truer story.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: a one-time viral read evicting genuinely hot keys
slides.markdown:
Under pure LRU, a single link shared widely for an hour and then never read again gets treated exactly like a genuinely popular, steadily-read item — both were "recently used." If the cache is full, LRU can evict a key that's read 1,000 times a day, every day, to make room for the viral one-off, simply because the viral read happened more recently.

This is the concrete failure LFU is designed to prevent: it would correctly keep the steady 1,000-reads-a-day key and let the one-off viral read, with its low accumulated count, get evicted instead.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: simulating both policies against real access logs
slides.markdown:
The right way to settle this isn't intuition — it's simulation against real traffic:

```
week_of_logs = access_log.load("last_7_days")

hit_rate_lru = simulate_cache(week_of_logs, policy="LRU", size=cache_size)
hit_rate_lfu = simulate_cache(week_of_logs, policy="LFU", size=cache_size)

print(f"LRU hit rate: {hit_rate_lru:.1%}")   # e.g. 78.2%
print(f"LFU hit rate: {hit_rate_lfu:.1%}")   # e.g. 91.4%
```

Running both policies offline against the same week of real traffic turns "I think LFU is better here" into a number you can defend — and sometimes the result surprises you either way.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
| LRU | LFU |
|---|---|
| Simple bookkeeping — a doubly linked list, O(1) per access | More bookkeeping — a running count per key, plus logic to decay old counts over time |
| Reacts instantly to changing access patterns | Slower to "forget" something that used to be popular but no longer is |

**How to decide:** LFU tracks true popularity better, but it costs more bookkeeping per access and needs a decay mechanism so yesterday's popularity doesn't permanently protect a key that's gone cold — without decay, LFU can be worse than LRU at adapting to genuinely shifting access patterns.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "how would you verify your choice was right after shipping it?"
slides.markdown:
Cache **hit-rate monitoring**, split by policy if you can A/B them, or before-and-after if you can't. A real jump in hit rate after switching from LRU to LFU (or vice versa) confirms the access pattern genuinely favored the new policy; no change, or a drop, tells you the assumption behind the switch was wrong.

The honest answer includes that this is a hypothesis you verify in production, not a one-time decision — access patterns can shift over time, and a policy that was right a year ago may not be right now.

Yes — a common pattern is **LRU within a size tier, LFU for promotion into a smaller, faster hot tier**: most of the cache runs simple LRU, but a small top tier is reserved for items that cross a frequency threshold, evicted by LFU logic. This gets LRU's cheap bookkeeping for the bulk of the cache while still protecting the genuinely hottest items from being displaced by recency alone.

Naming this hybrid approach shows you're not treating eviction policy as a single global switch — it can be tiered, matching different parts of the cache to different access patterns.

**Wrong belief:** "LRU is the standard eviction policy, so we'll use it here."

**Why it's wrong:** it skips checking whether the access pattern actually fits LRU's assumption — that recency predicts future access. For a trending or viral-prone workload, that assumption breaks down, and LRU can evict genuinely popular content in favor of a one-time spike, actively hurting the hit rate compared to a policy that fits the real pattern.

**Correct model:** name the access pattern first — recency-driven, frequency-driven, or time-bound — and let that pick the policy. "LRU is standard" is a reason to consider it, not a reason to skip the check.

LRU for recency-driven access, LFU for a stable hot set where sustained popularity beats raw recency, TTL for time-bound relevance. A viral one-off read can fool LRU into evicting genuinely popular content — LFU's accumulated count doesn't make that mistake, at the cost of more bookkeeping and needing a decay mechanism. Simulate against real access logs rather than guessing, monitor hit rate after shipping, and consider tiering LRU and LFU together instead of picking one globally.
